questions.prompt: Cinderline's CI pipeline deploys job definitions every night with nobody at the keyboard. Which identity should it authenticate as?

options.text: A shared user account such as ci@cinderline.example whose password the team knows.
options.rationale: A shared human account hides who acted, breaks when its password rotates, and gives a workload a person's identity.

options.text: The workspace administrator's personal access token, stored as a pipeline variable.
options.rationale: The pipeline would act with every administrator privilege, and every audit row would name the administrator instead of the pipeline.

options.text: A service principal created for deployment, holding only the grants deployment needs.
options.rationale: Service principals exist for jobs, scripts and CI/CD; a dedicated one can be scoped, rotated and audited without touching any person's access.

options.text: Whichever engineer's browser sign-in is still cached on the build agent.
options.rationale: A cached user-to-machine sign-in acts as that person, stops when their session or employment ends, and cannot be limited to deployment.

questions.prompt: Priya's identity-provider account is disabled when she leaves, and SCIM provisioning into the Databricks account is configured. What changes in Databricks, and what does not?

options.text: Nothing changes until a workspace admin deletes her separately in each workspace.
options.rationale: With account-level identities assigned to workspaces, the account is the source; per-workspace clean-up is the pattern identity federation replaces.

options.text: The sync removes her Databricks user, so her group-based access ends, while the groups' grants stay exactly as they were.
options.rationale: Documented: terminating a user in the identity provider removes the user from the account; grants attach to groups, which lose one member.

options.text: Her user is removed and the SELECT grants held by quality-analysts are revoked with her.
options.rationale: Removing a member never edits a group's grants; every other member keeps reading.

options.text: Token federation revokes her grants because her provider can no longer issue tokens for her.
options.rationale: Token federation only decides which issuer's tokens are accepted; it creates, removes and grants nothing.

questions.prompt: Maya's laptop is stolen a week after she ran databricks auth login on it. Which item on the laptop matters most, and what should happen?

options.text: The databricks-cli client ID, which must be rotated for every user.
options.rationale: databricks-cli names the OAuth client application and is the same for everyone; it is not a secret and grants nothing.

options.text: The PKCE verifier from her sign-in, which must be cancelled.
options.rationale: A PKCE verifier is made for one sign-in and is useless once that code exchange has happened.

options.text: Nothing, because U2M stores no credential on the device.
options.rationale: U2M deliberately caches tokens so later calls need no browser, and that cache is exactly what the thief now holds.

options.text: The cached refresh token, which can mint access tokens as Maya without a browser prompt; revoke her sessions and tokens.
options.rationale: The refresh token stays valid until it is revoked or expires, so revocation is the containment step for the lost device.

questions.prompt: A nightly script that authenticates with OAuth M2M starts failing at the token request itself. Its service principal's grants are unchanged and the network path is healthy. Where do you look first?

options.text: At the service principal's OAuth secret: its expiry time and status, then rotate it if it lapsed or was deleted.
options.rationale: A failure at the token request means the client ID or secret was refused; secrets have lifetimes and statuses that explain exactly this.

options.text: At the Unity Catalog grants on the target table.
options.rationale: A missing grant is reported by Unity Catalog after a token exists; this request never obtained one.

options.text: At the row filter on the table the script reads.
options.rationale: Row filters run at query time and change results; they cannot make the token request fail.

options.text: At the bearer header the script sends to the workspace API.
options.rationale: The header is used after the token request succeeds; the failure happened before any API call.

questions.prompt: The federation policy for sp-ci-deploy accepts the CI issuer and the subject repo:cinderline/quality-jobs:ref:refs/heads/main. A pull-request workflow in the same repository, whose token subject is repo:cinderline/quality-jobs:pull_request, asks for a Databricks token. What happens?

options.text: The exchange succeeds, because the issuer and the repository are the same.
options.rationale: The issuer is only one of the matched fields; the subject decides which workload may act as the service principal.

options.text: It succeeds only if the workflow also presents the service principal's OAuth secret.
options.rationale: Federation uses no Databricks secret at all; adding one would bring back the stored credential federation removes.

options.text: The exchange is refused, because the token's subject does not match the subject the policy names.
options.rationale: A service principal federation policy names the workload identity allowed to act as the principal; a different workflow context carries a different subject.

options.text: It receives a token for the pull-request author's user account instead.
options.rationale: A service principal federation policy maps an accepted token to that service principal, never to a person.

questions.prompt: Lena's personal access token was pasted into a notebook that was pushed to a private repository two days ago. She has since changed her password. Is the exposure contained?

options.text: Yes. Changing the password invalidates every token issued before it.
options.rationale: Tokens are created with their own lifetime and are revoked through the token APIs; a password reset is not a revocation.

options.text: No. The token is a separate bearer credential with its own lifetime, so it works until it expires or is revoked; revoke it now.
options.rationale: A token authenticates on its own; the password is a different credential, and only revocation or expiry ends the token.

options.text: Yes, once the file is removed from the repository's latest commit.
options.rationale: Git history and every existing clone still hold the old commit; hiding the file does not stop anyone who copied the token.

options.text: Only if the repository is public; a private repository keeps tokens safe.
options.rationale: Everyone with read access to a private repository, now or later, can use the token; private is not secret.

questions.prompt: The nightly job reads the SFTP password from scope supplier-sftp and fails with a permission error on the secrets call. The job runs as sp-nightly-ingest, a member of ingest-jobs. Which change is the narrow fix?

options.text: Grant MANAGE on the scope to ingest-jobs so the job can never be blocked again.
options.rationale: MANAGE also lets the job's identity change the ACL and write values, far beyond reading one secret.

options.text: Grant READ to the engineer who created the job.
options.rationale: The permission checked is that of the identity running the command, which is the service principal, not the job's creator.

options.text: Grant READ to the users group so every workspace member can read it.
options.rationale: users means all workspace users; it turns one integration's password into everyone's.

options.text: Grant READ on scope supplier-sftp to ingest-jobs.
options.rationale: READ is the least permission that lets a principal read a secret, and granting it to the group covers the service principal the job runs as.

questions.prompt: Ravi must be able to start the nightly job, which runs as sp-nightly-ingest, but must never change what it does or what it can reach. Which access fits?

options.text: Permission to manage and edit the job, so he can also fix it at night.
options.rationale: Edit rights let him change the code that then runs with the service principal's grants, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: A job permission to trigger and cancel runs, without edit rights on the job and without the servicePrincipal user role.
options.rationale: He can start the existing code, which runs with the service principal's grants, but can change neither the code nor the run-as identity.

options.text: The servicePrincipal user role on sp-nightly-ingest.
options.rationale: That role lets him make any job he controls run as the principal, handing him its grants indirectly.

options.text: MODIFY on quality.raw.deliveries for Ravi himself.
options.rationale: The run is checked against the service principal, so Ravi's own MODIFY is unnecessary and only adds direct write access.

questions.prompt: An analyst runs SELECT * FROM quality.accepted.inspections and gets zero rows with no error; yesterday the same query returned 40. Her grants are unchanged. Which layer is the likely cause, and what do you check first?

options.text: A missing SELECT privilege: check the table's grants.
options.rationale: A missing privilege raises PERMISSION_DENIED naming the privilege; it never returns an empty success.

options.text: The network path: check routes and DNS to the warehouse.
options.rationale: An unreachable path times out or fails to connect; it does not return a completed, empty query.

options.text: The row filter: check whether its function or her group memberships changed since yesterday.
options.rationale: An empty success is the signature of a filter returning false for her rows; grants cannot explain a result without an error.

options.text: An expired token: sign in again.
options.rationale: An expired credential fails authentication before the query runs, so no result of any size comes back.

questions.prompt: Maya is added to quality-leads and stays in plant-eu-analysts. With the plant_rows filter and inspector_email_mask functions from this beat, what does her SELECT * on inspections return?

options.text: All four rows with the stored emails, because the filter's first clause and the mask's condition both admit quality-leads.
options.rationale: The filter is one boolean expression joined by OR and the mask tests quality-leads membership; both are now true for Maya.

options.text: Only the two EU rows, because her plant group is checked first.
options.rationale: Clause order does not matter: whichever OR clause is true admits the row.

options.text: All four rows with masked emails, because a mask ignores group membership.
options.rationale: The mask's CASE expression tests quality-leads membership, which Maya now has.

options.text: PERMISSION_DENIED, because two filter clauses match the same caller.
options.rationale: Filters never raise errors; overlapping clauses simply both evaluate, and OR admits the row.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's mask_pii_columns policy on schema quality.accepted masks columns tagged pii for account users except quality-leads. With nobody editing the policy, which change stops it protecting the email column of supplier_contacts?

options.text: A new table is created in the same schema.
options.rationale: New tables beneath the schema are within the policy's scope; only untagged columns escape it.

options.text: Maya moves from plant-eu-analysts to finance-analysts.
options.rationale: The policy applies to account users except quality-leads, so Maya is masked in either group.

options.text: The ownership of supplier_contacts passes to another group.
options.rationale: Ownership does not change which columns the policy's tag condition matches.

options.text: Someone allowed to assign tags removes the pii tag from that column.
options.rationale: The policy matches columns by tag, so an untagged column falls outside it; tag assignment is therefore a governed permission.

questions.prompt: Security asks whether any identity other than sp-nightly-ingest read the supplier SFTP password this week. Which approach answers it?

options.text: Read the scope's ACL; nobody without READ can have read it.
options.rationale: The ACL shows who could read, not who did, and it cannot show a READ holder who used it.

options.text: Query system.access.audit for the week's secrets-service getSecret rows whose request parameters name scope supplier-sftp, grouped by acting identity.
options.rationale: Secret reads are recorded as secrets-service events with the acting identity; grouping by identity isolates anyone other than the service principal.

options.text: Search notebook outputs for the redaction marker.
options.rationale: Redaction markers appear only where a value was printed, and a transformed value is not redacted at all.

options.text: Query the billing system table for jobs that ran this week.
options.rationale: Billing rows record usage quantities, not which identity read which secret.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline finds 40 direct user grants on quality tables, added one at a time over two years. Describe how you would move to group-based grants without cutting off anyone's legitimate access, and what evidence shows the move is safe.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Export the current grants and memberships, then cluster the 40 users by the access they actually use, confirmed with their managers and recent audit rows. Create or reuse account groups per role, maintained by SCIM, and grant each group its privileges on the lowest securable that works. Add the users to the groups, run the access test matrix as representative members to prove the group path works, and only then revoke the direct grants in batches. Re-run the matrix after each batch, including the must-fail rows, and keep the before and after grant lists as evidence.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Adding the group path before removing direct grants avoids an outage, and the matrix plus audit rows show both that nothing legitimate broke and that nothing new opened. Migrating team by team instead of all at once is an acceptable alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the first five actions, in order, for Cinderline's leaked-token incident. For each, name who performs it and the evidence it produces or preserves.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: First, Lena or a workspace admin revokes the token, and the revocation time is recorded because it closes the exposure window. Second, security fixes the window from the token's creation time and the commit time to the revocation. Third, security queries the audit rows for Lena's identity inside that window and saves the result with the query time, noting unfamiliar source addresses. Fourth, the platform owner lists what Lena's grants and secret ACLs could reach. Fifth, the owners of every secret she could read rotate it, and the incident log records each change.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Revocation first stops further use; each later step depends on the window and the reach it establishes, and saving query results with timestamps keeps the evidence reproducible. Notifying the security owner before step three is an acceptable variation.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's platform administrator proposes to approve and apply her own request for MANAGE on the quality catalog, to save time during an audit. Explain which duties should be separated here, who should hold each, and what evidence closes the change.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Requesting, approving, applying and reviewing are four duties. The administrator may request, but the catalog owner or security owner approves, a second platform administrator applies it, and security reviews the resulting audit row for the permission change. Before approval, the request should state why a narrower privilege such as SELECT on the audit tables is not enough, and name an expiry. Evidence is the approved request, the updatePermissions audit row, the test matrix run afterwards and the revocation at expiry.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Self-approval removes the only independent check on a broad privilege, and MANAGE lets its holder change grants for others. Where only one administrator exists, an acceptable alternative is a time-boxed grant with mandatory after-the-fact review by security.

beats.title: People and workloads need different identities
beats.outcome: Classify each actor in a request as a user, a service principal or a group, and say which one should run production work.
beats.explanation: Databricks recognises three kinds of principal. A [[dbxfe-identity-user-concept|user]] is a person, identified by an email address. A [[dbxfe-identity-sp-concept|service principal]] is an identity for jobs, scripts, apps and CI/CD, with no person behind it. A group collects users, service principals and other groups so access is granted once. The Databricks SDK's own guidance is to run production jobs as service principals, so people need no write privilege in production. Notice in the second state that Lena's personal write path disappears while the nightly job keeps writing.

handbook.markdown:
**Three principal types.** A user is a person, identified by an email address and normally provisioned from the identity provider. A service principal is identified by an application ID, and OAuth calls present that ID as the client ID. The Terraform provider's documentation separates Databricks-managed service principals, which exist only inside Databricks on every cloud and cannot reach other services, from Azure-managed ones registered from Microsoft Entra ID; Cinderline on AWS uses Databricks-managed ones. A group has no credential of its own; it exists to receive grants and entitlements.

**Account and workspace.** Identities live in the Databricks account and are assigned to workspaces with USER or ADMIN permission. Workspace entitlements, such as workspace access or SQL access, are set separately from Unity Catalog privileges, so being able to open a workspace says nothing about reading a table.

**Why workloads get their own identity.** The SDK's description of service principals gives the reason: if every process that changes production data runs as a service principal, interactive users need no write, delete or modify privilege there, and nobody overwrites production by accident. Audit rows also become honest: a nightly write recorded under Lena's email cannot be told apart from Lena typing it.

**Inspect it.** Ask the platform which identity a session authenticated as:

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
w = WorkspaceClient()        # credentials come from the environment, never from source code
me = w.current_user.me()     # the authenticated user or service principal
print(me.user_name, me.display_name)
```

**Limits.** A service principal is not automatically least privilege: it holds exactly what its groups and grants give it, and the provider documents adding one to the admins group, which makes it an administrator. One service principal per workload, named for its purpose, keeps blast radius and audit trails readable.

beats.recap: People get users, workloads get service principals, and groups carry the grants.

beats.title: Grant to the group, then move people between groups
beats.outcome: Predict how a membership change alters a principal's access without touching any grant.
beats.explanation: A grant names a principal; when that principal is a [[dbxfe-identity-group-concept|group]], every member inherits it, including service principals and nested groups. Cinderline grants the accepted schema's read privileges to quality-analysts and never to Maya directly; plant-eu-analysts sits inside quality-analysts. When Maya moves from the EU plant team to finance, an identity administrator changes one membership and her read access follows. Notice that the grants table is the same in every state: only membership changed, and her effective access changed with it.

samajh.text: Socho society ke gate par guard ke paas ek list hai: 'Tower B ke residents andar aa sakte hain.' Kisi resident ka naam alag se nahi likha. Maya Tower B se Tower D shift hui, toh society office ne sirf uska tower badla. Guard ki list wahi rahi, par Maya ab Tower B wale gate se andar nahi aati. Access naam se nahi, membership se chalta hai.
samajh.mapping: The guard's list is a grant to a group, Tower B is the group, and moving towers is changing group membership.
samajh.boundary: A society office is one authority; in Databricks, memberships often come from the identity provider through SCIM and take effect only after the next sync.

beats.hint: Compare the grants table in the last state with the first two: which column moved?
beats.recap: Grant once to a group; membership, not the grant, decides who reads.

beats.title: SCIM moves identities; federation decides which token is trusted
beats.outcome: Tell SCIM provisioning, workspace identity federation and token federation apart by what each one moves or trusts.
beats.explanation: Three mechanisms are easily blurred. [[dbxfe-identity-scim-concept|SCIM provisioning]] copies users, groups and memberships from Cinderline's identity provider into the Databricks account and removes a user who is deprovisioned there. [[dbxfe-identity-federation-concept|Identity federation]] means those account identities are assigned to workspaces instead of being recreated in each one. Token federation lets Databricks accept a token issued by a trusted identity provider and exchange it for a Databricks token. Notice in the diagram that only the SCIM sync creates or removes a principal, and that none of the three grants a privilege.

handbook.markdown:
**Four mechanisms, four jobs.**

| Mechanism | Moves or trusts | Creates or removes principals? | Grants privileges? |
|---|---|---|---|
| SCIM provisioning | users, groups and memberships from the identity provider | yes | no |
| Identity federation | account identities assigned to workspaces as USER or ADMIN | no | workspace access only |
| Account token federation | tokens from a trusted issuer, exchanged for Databricks tokens | no | no |
| Workload identity federation | one workload's platform token, for one service principal | no | no |

Single sign-on is a separate idea: it answers how a person proves who they are when signing in. SCIM answers which identities exist at all.

**Evidence in the APIs.** The SDK recommends SCIM provisioning and states that terminating a user in the identity provider removes the user from the Databricks account. Its user fields note that with identity federation enabled, attributes such as the display name are updated through the account SCIM APIs, not the workspace ones: the account is the source of truth. The account federation policy API describes token federation as exchanging identity-provider tokens for Databricks OAuth tokens, typically combined with SCIM so the users already exist.

**What to inspect.** The identity provider's sync log for the change; the account's user and group lists; the workspace assignment of the group; the federation policy's issuer and subject mapping. When access is wrong, find which of the four made the difference before touching a grant.

**Limits.** Connectors differ by identity provider in what they sync, such as nested groups or service principals; the Azure module covers Microsoft Entra ID specifics. A sync runs on a schedule, so offboarding has a delay, and deprovisioning a person does not by itself review the service principals and jobs that person managed.

beats.recap: SCIM decides who exists, federation decides whose tokens are trusted, and grants decide access.

beats.title: U2M lets a tool act as the person who signed in
beats.outcome: Trace an OAuth user-to-machine sign-in from browser consent to a cached refresh token and name whose permissions the tool uses.
beats.explanation: In [[dbxfe-identity-u2m-concept|OAuth user-to-machine (U2M)]] sign-in, a tool such as the Databricks CLI opens the workspace's sign-in page in a browser. After Maya signs in, the browser returns an authorization code to a listener on her laptop, and the tool exchanges it, with a one-time PKCE verifier, for an access token and a refresh token that it caches. Every later call acts as Maya, with Maya's grants. Notice on the timeline that no password or long-lived token is typed into the tool, and that the cached refresh token becomes the thing to protect.

handbook.markdown:
**The flow, as the Python SDK implements it.** The external-browser strategy uses the databricks-cli client ID unless another is configured, creates a PKCE verifier and an S256 challenge, opens the authorization page, and listens on http://localhost:8020 for the redirect. The code and verifier are exchanged for tokens; because the request includes offline_access, a refresh token is issued, and tokens are cached under the SDK's own directory in the user's home folder. The SDK comments that offline_access only decides whether a refresh token is issued and grants no API permission.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
w = WorkspaceClient(host="https://<workspace-url>", auth_type="external-browser")
for t in w.tables.list(catalog_name="quality", schema_name="accepted"):
    print(t.full_name)   # only tables Maya may see
```

The Terraform provider documents the same pattern from the CLI: after `databricks auth login`, tools reuse the cached OAuth token of that profile.

**Whose permissions apply.** Maya's, always: the token represents her, so Unity Catalog checks her grants and group memberships. The client ID names the tool, not a principal with privileges.

**What to protect.** The refresh token on disk can mint new access tokens without a browser prompt until it is revoked or expires, so the laptop's disk is now part of the credential. Do not copy the cache into containers or shared machines; sign out and revoke sessions when a device is lost.

**When U2M is wrong.** Unattended jobs: a person's session stops when the person leaves, and the job would act with everything the person can reach. Use M2M or workload identity federation for workloads.

beats.recap: U2M signs a person in once; the cached refresh token then acts as that person.

beats.title: M2M trades a service principal's secret for a short-lived token
beats.outcome: Describe the OAuth client-credentials exchange a service principal performs and locate the two places it can fail.
beats.explanation: In [[dbxfe-identity-m2m-concept|OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M)]] authentication, the caller sends the service principal's client ID, which is its application ID, and an OAuth secret to the Databricks token endpoint. It receives an access token with an expiry and sends that token as a bearer header on each API call; the SDK refreshes it shortly before it expires. Notice the two failure points in the diagram: a wrong or expired secret fails at the token endpoint, while a valid token without a grant fails later, at Unity Catalog.

samajh.text: Office mein ek vendor ka courier roz aata hai. Uske paas company ka ek permanent letter hai. Har subah woh reception par letter dikhata hai aur ek din ka visitor pass leta hai; andar har darwaza sirf pass dekhta hai. Pass shaam ko khud expire ho jata hai. Letter ki bhi expiry date hai: purana letter reception par hi rok diya jata hai, andar ke darwazon tak baat pahunchti hi nahi.
samajh.mapping: The permanent letter is the service principal's OAuth secret, reception is the token endpoint, and the day pass is the access token each API checks.
samajh.boundary: Real tokens are signed and scoped and the SDK refreshes them automatically; a visitor pass also does not decide which rooms' data you may read, which grants do.

beats.hint: Ask whether the failing request ever received a token.

handbook.markdown:
**The exchange.** The SDK's oauth-m2m strategy needs a host, a client ID and a client secret. It discovers endpoints at `/oidc/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`, posts `grant_type=client_credentials` to the token endpoint (`/oidc/v1/token`) with the scope `all-apis` unless configured otherwise, and adds `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to every request, refreshing the token 40 seconds before its expiry.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed. The runner injects the variables.
import os
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
w = WorkspaceClient(
    host=os.environ["DATABRICKS_HOST"],
    client_id=os.environ["DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID"],          # sp-nightly-ingest's application ID
    client_secret=os.environ["DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET"],  # never written in code or notebooks
)
```

The SDK marks the secret as sensitive, so its configuration debug output prints `***` instead of the value.

**Secrets have lifetimes.** Administrators create OAuth secrets for a service principal; the provider documents a default lifetime of 730 days when none is set, and every secret reports its creation time, expiry time and status. A script that worked for two years and then fails at the token request is the expected symptom of a lapsed secret. Rotate by creating a second secret, switching the workload, confirming it, then deleting the first.

**Credential scope.** The scope bounds which APIs a token is issued for; the grants bound which data the principal reaches. Neither replaces the other, and neither is widened to fix a refusal from the other.

**Two failure points.** Authentication errors arrive before any object is named: check the secret, its status and the host. PERMISSION_DENIED naming a privilege arrives after authentication succeeded: check the principal's grants, not the secret.

beats.recap: Client ID plus secret buys a bearer token; a bad secret fails early, a missing grant fails late.

beats.title: Workload identity federation removes the stored secret
beats.outcome: Explain how a CI job authenticates as a service principal without any Databricks secret, and which policy fields decide whether its token is accepted.
beats.explanation: With [[dbxfe-identity-wif-concept|workload identity federation]], Cinderline's CI runner asks its own platform for a signed identity token and exchanges it at the Databricks token endpoint for an OAuth token for sp-ci-deploy. A service principal federation policy decides acceptance: the issuer must match, the subject must name the permitted workload, such as one repository's main branch, and the audience must match. Databricks' SDK recommends this over OAuth secrets or personal access tokens whenever possible. Notice in the second state that a pull-request run from the same repository carries a different subject and is refused.

handbook.markdown:
**The exchange.** The SDK's OIDC strategies obtain a JWT from the workload's platform and send it to the Databricks token endpoint with the token-exchange grant (`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, subject token type JWT). With a client ID, the exchange authenticates as that service principal; the code comments that there is no rotatable secret in this flow. Without a client ID it is account-wide token federation for users.

**The policy.** A service principal federation policy names the issuer (the `iss` claim, an https URL), the subject (the `sub` claim unless another claim is configured) and optionally the audiences, which default to the Databricks account ID. Signing keys are normally discovered from the issuer's well-known endpoint. The provider's pages for both federation policy resources carry a GA release-stage badge at v1.133.0; the SDK lists GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Terraform Cloud and Kubernetes among supported platforms.

```yaml
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed. A GitHub Actions job.
permissions:
  id-token: write        # lets the job request an identity token from the CI platform
env:
  DATABRICKS_HOST: https://<workspace-url>
  DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: <sp-ci-deploy application ID>
  DATABRICKS_AUTH_TYPE: github-oidc
```

The subject format belongs to the CI platform; the ones in this beat follow GitHub's pattern and are synthetic.

**Why it is preferred.** Nothing long-lived is stored in CI, so there is nothing to leak from CI variables or logs, and nothing to rotate. The SDK states that Databricks strongly recommends it over OAuth client secrets or personal access tokens whenever possible.

**Limits.** A broad subject lets any branch or pull request act as the service principal; match the narrowest workload that deploys. Federation authenticates; the service principal's grants still decide what the deploy can touch.

beats.recap: Federation swaps a stored secret for an issuer-and-subject match on each run.

beats.title: Whoever holds a bearer token is its owner
beats.outcome: Name the common ways a token leaks and say why each gives the finder the owner's full access.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-identity-pat-concept|personal access token]] (PAT) is a bearer credential: the API checks that the token is valid and then acts as whoever it was issued to. It cannot tell Lena from someone who copied her token. Tokens leak in predictable places: a notebook cell that is later committed, a job's debug output, a URL, a chat message. Notice in the table that every leak path gives the finder Lena's grants, not a reduced set, and that only revocation ends them all. That is why Databricks recommends OAuth over personal access tokens.

samajh.text: PAT ek ghar ki extra chaabi jaisa hai. Jiske haath mein chaabi, darwaza usi ke liye khulta hai; tala yeh nahi poochta ki chaabi kisne banwayi. Chaabi ki photo family group mein daal di toh har member ke paas copy aa gayi. Photo delete karne se copy wapas nahi aati. Tala badalna, yaani token revoke karna, hi pakka ilaaj hai.
samajh.mapping: The key is a bearer personal access token, the lock is the API, and posting the photo is committing the token to a repository or chat.
samajh.boundary: A key opens one door, while a token opens every API its owner may use; a token can also expire on its own, which a key never does.

beats.hint: List who could read the token, not who was meant to.

handbook.markdown:
**Bearer means possession is enough.** A personal access token is created for the authenticated user with a lifetime in seconds; on AWS and Google Cloud an administrator can also create on-behalf-of tokens for a service principal. The provider's documentation states that Databricks strongly recommends OAuth instead of personal access tokens for user authentication, and that OAuth with a client ID and secret is generally better for service principals, keeping on-behalf-of tokens for integrations that cannot use OAuth.

**Token exposure mistakes.**

| Mistake | Why it is dangerous |
|---|---|
| Token as a literal in a notebook or script | The file travels: Git, exports, copies |
| `print(token)` while debugging a job | Run output is readable by everyone who can view the run |
| Token on a command line | Shell history and process listings keep it |
| Token in a URL | Proxies and logs record full URLs |
| One long-lived token shared by a team | Nobody can tell who acted; rotation breaks everyone |

The SDK itself treats `token` and `client_secret` as sensitive and prints `***` in its configuration debug string; your own code must do the same.

**Controls that exist.** Token use is itself a permission (CAN_USE on the workspace's tokens object), so a workspace can limit who may create tokens at all. Administrators can list every token and delete any user's token; each record carries its creator, creation time, expiry time and an approximate last-used day, accurate to one day, which bounds an incident.

**What is not a control.** Rewriting Git history, deleting a chat message or making a repository private does not un-leak a token that was already readable. Changing the owner's password does not revoke it. Revoke first; clean up second.

beats.recap: A bearer token is the owner in anyone's hands; revoke it, never just hide it.

beats.title: A secret scope decides who may read a value, not what they do with it
beats.outcome: Design a secret scope ACL with READ, WRITE and MANAGE and explain why redaction is not a control.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-identity-scope-concept|secret scope]] stores values such as the supplier's SFTP password, and its ACL grants READ, WRITE or MANAGE to users, groups or service principals. Code reads a value at run time through the secrets utility, and the permission checked is that of whoever runs the command. Databricks redacts secret values it recognises in notebook output, but its SDK states plainly that a user allowed to read a secret can reveal it. Notice that ingest-jobs holds READ only, and that only the platform owners can change the ACL.

samajh.text: Bank locker socho. Locker room mein kaun ja sakta hai, yeh bank ka register tay karta hai: kuch log sirf dekh sakte hain, kuch saaman rakh bhi sakte hain, aur manager naye naam jod sakta hai. Par ek baar haar locker se bahar aa gaya, toh pehenne wala use kisi ko bhi dikha sakta hai. Bank ki zimmedari wahin khatam ho jaati hai.
samajh.mapping: The bank's list is the secret scope ACL with READ, WRITE and MANAGE, the necklace is the secret value, and wearing it outside is a job copying a secret it was allowed to read.
samajh.boundary: Databricks also redacts secret values it recognises in notebook output, which a bank cannot do, but that redaction is best effort and not a control.

beats.hint: Which permission lets a principal read without letting it change who else may read?

handbook.markdown:
**Permissions, strongest first.** The SDK's ACL call orders them: MANAGE may change ACLs and read and write; WRITE may read and write; READ may read the scope and list its secrets. A principal uses the strongest permission it holds. The scope's creator receives MANAGE unless the scope is created with `users` as the initial manage principal, which the provider documents as meaning all workspace users.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed. Runs inside a job as sp-nightly-ingest.
password = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="supplier-sftp", key="password")
client = connect_sftp(host=SFTP_HOST, user="cinderline", password=password)  # hypothetical helper
# Never print, log, return or write the value.
```

A value can also be referenced in Spark configuration or environment variables as `{{secrets/supplier-sftp/password}}`, which keeps it out of code entirely.

**Where the value can be read.** Only from within a command on a cluster, with the permission of whoever runs that command; there is no API that returns the value to a laptop. Writing a secret needs WRITE or MANAGE. The provider lists limits of 128 KB per value and 1000 secrets per scope.

**Redaction is best effort.** The SDK's own description says that Databricks makes an effort to redact secret values displayed in notebooks, but it is not possible to prevent users with permission from reading them. A reader can transform or copy a value, so the ACL is the control and redaction is a convenience.

**Credential scope as a design rule.** One scope per integration keeps READ on the SFTP password from also exposing the ERP password. Give MANAGE to the few owners, READ to the group of the workload's principal, and nothing to users. Every read is an audit event, which the audit beat queries.

beats.recap: The ACL decides who reads a secret; after that, only trust protects the value.

beats.title: The run-as identity, not the person who clicked Run, meets the grants
beats.outcome: Identify the acting principal for an interactive query, a scheduled job run and a run that someone else triggers.
beats.explanation: Unity Catalog checks the [[dbxfe-identity-runas-concept|acting principal]], which is not always the person at the keyboard. An interactive notebook query acts as its user. A job acts as its run-as identity; when none is set, the SDK documents that it runs as its creator. So when Ravi presses Run now on the nightly job, its reads and writes still happen as sp-nightly-ingest. Making a service principal the run-as identity requires the servicePrincipal user role on it. Notice how the three paths in the diagram reach a table as different principals.
beats.hint: Separate the permission on the job from the privilege on the table.

handbook.markdown:
**Three acting principals.** Interactive work acts as the signed-in user. A job acts as its run-as identity: the SDK's job settings describe the run-as field as naming the user or service principal the job runs as, and without it the job runs as the user who created it. The reported run-as user defaults to the creator, or to the owner when job access control is enabled. The permission to view, trigger, cancel or manage a job is a separate job permission.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
w = WorkspaceClient()
job = w.jobs.get(job_id=123)     # hypothetical job ID
print(job.run_as_user_name)      # a user email or a service principal's application ID
```

**Indirect access to review.**

| Held by Ravi | What it lets him do |
|---|---|
| Permission to trigger the job | run the job's existing code as sp-nightly-ingest |
| Permission to edit the job | change the code that then runs as sp-nightly-ingest |
| servicePrincipal user role on the principal | make a job he controls run as it |

The last two amount to holding the service principal's grants. An access review that lists only direct grants misses them.

**Setting run-as.** Making a service principal the run-as identity requires the servicePrincipal/user role, and account rule sets keep `roles/servicePrincipal.user` apart from `roles/servicePrincipal.manager`, which manages the principal itself. Give the user role to the few who deploy the job, not to everyone who may trigger it.

**Inspect.** The job's run-as setting and permission list, the service principal's rule set, and audit rows, which name the principal that performed each action. **Limits.** Other objects, such as published dashboards and apps, have their own identity rules; read each one's page rather than assuming the caller's identity applies.

beats.recap: Grants are checked against the acting principal; a job's is its run-as identity.

beats.title: Each layer refuses in its own words
beats.outcome: Place a failed request at the credential, workspace, catalog, data-policy, secret or network layer from what it returned.
beats.explanation: One request passes several [[dbxfe-identity-layer-concept|layers]], and each fails differently. A bad or expired credential fails authentication before any object is named. A principal not assigned to the workspace is stopped there. A missing USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA or SELECT returns PERMISSION_DENIED naming the privilege. A row filter or column mask raises nothing: it returns fewer rows or replaced values. A secret ACL refuses the secrets call, and an unreachable path times out. Notice which state in the diagram ends with a successful, empty result.
beats.hint: Ask first whether the request produced an error at all.

handbook.markdown:
**Read the shape before the words.**

| Layer | What comes back | First check | Never the fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credential | authentication error, no object named | token or secret expiry and status, host | a new grant |
| Workspace | refused before any catalog check | workspace assignment and entitlements | ALL PRIVILEGES |
| Catalog privilege | PERMISSION_DENIED naming a privilege and securable | grants of the acting principal, parents included | admin group membership |
| Data policy | success with fewer rows or masked values | filter and mask functions, group memberships | dropping the filter |
| Secret ACL | PERMISSION_DENIED on the secrets call | scope ACL for the acting principal | MANAGE on the scope |
| Network | timeout or connection error, no refusal text | route, DNS, private connectivity | any permission change |

**The order.** Read the exact error and note whether it names an object. Identify the acting principal: user, run-as identity or service principal. Reproduce as that principal, never as an administrator whose success proves nothing. Fix one layer, then re-run the failing request and one request that must still fail.

**Worked case.** Jon's query on a new schema returns `PERMISSION_DENIED` naming USE SCHEMA. Authentication passed (the error names an object), so the fix is USE SCHEMA on quality.returns for the plant-us-analysts group, followed by the query and a must-fail check that Jon still cannot read `quality.raw`. If the same query returned zero rows instead, no grant would change it; the row filter would.

**Limits.** Wording varies by client and interface, and some tools wrap errors; rely on whether an object and privilege are named, not on exact text. Network diagnosis belongs to the cloud modules.

beats.recap: Authentication names no object, a privilege refusal names one, and a filter raises nothing.

beats.title: Filters and masks change the answer, not the permission
beats.outcome: Predict the rows and values two principals receive from one query on a table with a row filter and a column mask.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-identity-rowfilter-concept|row filter]] is a SQL function attached to a table that returns true for each row the caller may see; a [[dbxfe-identity-mask-concept|column mask]] is a function attached to one column that returns either the stored value or a replacement. Both run at query time for whoever is querying, and neither raises an error. Notice in the tables that Maya, an EU analyst, gets two rows with masked inspector emails, while Ravi, a quality lead, gets all four rows unmasked from the same statement.

samajh.text: School ka ek hi result register socho. Parents-teacher meeting mein har parent ko sirf apne bachche ki line dikhai jaati hai, baaki lines dhak di jaati hain. Aur teacher ke personal phone number ki jagah likha hota hai 'office se sampark karein'. Register ek hi hai, format sab ke liye same; bas har dekhne wale ko uske hisaab se hissa dikhta hai.
samajh.mapping: The register is the stored table, showing each parent only their child's line is the row filter, and replacing the phone number is the column mask, both decided by who is looking.
samajh.boundary: A teacher decides by recognising the parent; Unity Catalog decides by functions evaluated against the caller's identity at query time, and it never keeps a separate copy per viewer.

handbook.markdown:
**Attach them.** The dbt-databricks adapter emits exactly these statements, and its tests create filter functions that return BOOLEAN and mask functions that return the column's type:

```sql
-- Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION quality.governance.plant_rows(plant STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN is_account_group_member('quality-leads')
    OR (is_account_group_member('plant-eu-analysts') AND plant IN ('EU-1', 'EU-2'));

ALTER TABLE quality.accepted.inspections
  SET ROW FILTER quality.governance.plant_rows ON (plant);

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION quality.governance.inspector_email_mask(email STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('quality-leads') THEN email ELSE '[masked]' END;

ALTER TABLE quality.accepted.inspections
  ALTER COLUMN inspector_email SET MASK quality.governance.inspector_email_mask;
```

The membership test `is_account_group_member` is the pattern the row filters page describes; it was not re-read in this build, so confirm it, including how it treats nested groups, before relying on it.

**Mechanism.** The SDK's table types record a filter as a function name plus the columns passed to it, whose types must match, and a mask as a function whose first argument has the masked column's type, optionally with more columns. The stored table is unchanged; each query runs the functions for its own caller.

**Inspect.** `information_schema.row_filters` lists a table's filter and target columns; `system.information_schema.column_masks` lists masked columns and mask names.

**Test honestly.** Run the same query as each kind of principal and record row counts and a sampled value; an administrator's full result proves nothing. Include a principal the filter should see nothing for, because an empty result is the silent failure.

**Limits.** A mask is not encryption; the stored value is intact. Supported compute, runtimes and access paths have explicit limits, and neither feature works on the Hive metastore. The functions are code: they need an owner, a review and tests.

beats.recap: A filter removes rows and a mask replaces values, per caller, without an error.

beats.title: An attribute-based policy follows the tag, not the table
beats.outcome: Decide when one attribute-based policy on a schema can replace per-table masks, and name what must be verified before relying on it.
beats.explanation: Per-table masks are attached table by table, so a new table with an email column starts unprotected. An [[dbxfe-identity-abac-concept|attribute-based access control (ABAC)]] policy is defined once on a catalog, schema or table and applies to that securable and everything beneath it: it matches columns by governance tag, applies a row filter or column mask function, and names the principals it applies to and exempts. Creating one requires MANAGE on the securable. Notice in the second state that a new tagged table is masked without anyone touching it, and that an untagged column is not.
beats.hint: Look at what the policy's condition tests.

handbook.markdown:
**Components.** The provider's ABAC policy resource and the SDK's Policies API agree on the parts: conditions on governance tags and the caller's identity, an action (a row filter or a column mask function), a scope (a catalog, a schema or a table, applying to all descendants), principals the policy applies to and principals excepted, and a MANAGE requirement on the securable for anyone who views, creates, changes or deletes a policy.

```hcl
# Synthetic teaching example following the provider's documented shape; not applied.
resource "databricks_policy_info" "mask_pii_columns" {
  on_securable_type     = "SCHEMA"
  on_securable_fullname = "quality.accepted"
  name                  = "mask_pii_columns"
  policy_type           = "POLICY_TYPE_COLUMN_MASK"
  for_securable_type    = "TABLE"
  to_principals         = ["account users"]
  except_principals     = ["quality-leads"]
  when_condition        = "hasTag('pii')"
  match_columns         = [{ condition = "hasTag('pii')", alias = "pii_col" }]
  column_mask = {
    function_name = "quality.governance.redact_string"
    on_column     = "pii_col"
  }
}
```

The mask function's first argument and return type should match the masked column, as with a table-level mask.

**What moves.** The control shifts from "who attached a mask" to "who tags columns correctly". Governed tags are managed through tag policies, and account rule sets include separate tag policy creator, manager and assigner roles, so assigning a tag is itself a governed permission. Separate the people who write policies from the people who tag data, and test with an untagged column as a must-fail case.

**Status and limits.** The provider's page for this resource carried a GA release-stage badge when read on 2026-09-23. The product documentation's own status label, supported compute and regional availability were not read in this build; verify them for Cinderline's workspace before promising the feature. The API also lists grant and deny policy types, which this module does not rely on. Read the current rules before combining a table-level mask and a policy on the same column.

beats.recap: One policy on a schema masks every tagged column beneath it; the tag is the control.

beats.title: An audit row joins an identity to an action and its response
beats.outcome: Write a query over the audit log that answers who did what, when, from where and with what result, and state what it cannot show.
beats.explanation: The [[dbxfe-identity-audit-concept|audit log system table]], system.access.audit, records account and workspace events as rows: the time, the workspace, a service and action name, the identity that acted, request parameters, the source address and the response. An account admin enables the access system schema first, and reading it should itself be a narrow grant. Notice in the second state how one filter isolates the only permission change, and that no row records what anyone did with data after reading it.

handbook.markdown:
**Enable, then grant narrowly.** The provider documents that system tables must be enabled by an account admin, schema by schema, with the access schema as its example; the SDK describes system schemas as holding usage information such as audit logs. Grant read on the audit table to a security group, not to everyone: it lists who touched what.

**Query shape.** Column names below are recalled from the audit log reference and were not re-read in this build; confirm them before evidence depends on a query.

```sql
-- Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
SELECT user_identity.email AS actor,
       count(*)            AS reads,
       min(event_time)     AS first_read,
       max(event_time)     AS last_read
FROM system.access.audit
WHERE service_name = 'secrets'
  AND action_name  = 'getSecret'
  AND request_params['scope'] = 'supplier-sftp'
  AND event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS
GROUP BY user_identity.email;
```

The same pattern answers "who changed grants" with `service_name = 'unityCatalog'` and the permission-change action, and "what did this identity do" with a filter on the actor and a time window, reading `source_ip_address` and `user_agent` for unfamiliar origins.

**A second channel.** On AWS, audit logs can also be delivered as JSON files to Cinderline's own S3 bucket. The provider documents availability within 15 minutes of activation, new files every few minutes, occasional later arrivals, and files that may be rewritten with extra lines. Evidence gathered minutes after an event can therefore be incomplete: record the query time with the result.

**What it cannot show.** What a user did with rows after reading them, what a notebook printed, or whether a person or a copied token was behind a request. A row tied to sp-nightly-ingest shows the principal that acted, not who edited the job. Combine audit rows with job change history and the identity provider's sign-in log.

beats.recap: Audit rows tie identities to actions and responses, and say nothing about intent or later use.

beats.title: Contain a leaked token first, then reconstruct what it did
beats.outcome: Order the first actions after a token exposure and name the evidence each step preserves.
beats.explanation: When Lena's token is found in a repository, order matters. Revoke it first, because every minute spent analysing is a minute the finder can still act as her. Then fix the [[dbxfe-identity-incident-concept|exposure window]]: from the moment it could be copied until it was revoked. Query the audit rows for her identity inside that window, looking for unfamiliar source addresses and actions she would not take, and list everything her grants could reach. Record each step with its time. Notice where on the timeline evidence collection starts: after revocation, never before.

samajh.text: ATM card kho gaya toh pehla phone bank ko: card block karo. Uske baad statement dekhte ho ki kab, kahan aur kitna nikla. Pehle statement padhne baith gaye toh tab tak aur paisa nikal sakta hai. Aur nayi card ke liye kisi ko poore account ka control nahi de dete, sirf nayi card banti hai.
samajh.mapping: Blocking the card is revoking the token, reading the statement is querying audit rows inside the exposure window, and the new card is a narrowly scoped replacement credential.
samajh.boundary: A bank statement is complete and final; audit rows arrive with some delay and do not show what was done with data after it was read.

beats.hint: What is the one step that stops further damage while you analyse?

handbook.markdown:
**1. Contain.** The owner revokes the token through the Token API, or an administrator deletes it through token management, which lets admins list and delete any user's tokens. Deleting the commit, making the repository private or changing Lena's password contains nothing.

**2. Fix the window.** The token record carries its creation time, expiry time, creator and an approximate last-used day accurate to one day. The window runs from the earliest moment the token could be copied (here the commit, 12 September 17:20) to revocation (15 September 08:05). A last-used day after the commit is a strong signal to dig.

**3. Query the evidence.**

```sql
-- Synthetic teaching example; not executed. Column names as recalled from the audit reference.
SELECT event_time, service_name, action_name, source_ip_address, user_agent,
       response.status_code
FROM system.access.audit
WHERE user_identity.email = 'lena@cinderline.example'
  AND event_time BETWEEN '2026-09-12T17:20:00Z' AND '2026-09-15T08:05:00Z'
ORDER BY event_time;
```

Save the result with the time the query ran; delivery can lag, so re-run it later and compare.

**4. List the blast radius.** Everything Lena's groups, direct grants and secret ACLs reach, plus jobs that run as her. Anything she could read, especially secrets, is treated as exposed.

**5. Rotate and remove the cause.** Rotate readable secrets, move the nightly job to a service principal, restrict who holds CAN_USE on tokens, and prefer OAuth or workload identity federation for scripts.

**Separation of duties.** The responder who revokes does not grant replacement access; the owner of each secret rotates it; security reviews the audit evidence. Follow Cinderline's own incident process for notification. This sequence is teaching guidance, not a compliance procedure.

beats.recap: Revoke, bound the window, query inside it, list the reach, rotate, then fix the cause.

beats.title: A narrow plan ships with the tests that would catch it being wide
beats.outcome: Write a least-privilege plan as a principal-securable-action matrix with must-fail rows, and assign request, approval, application and audit to different people.
beats.explanation: A threat and access review ends in two artifacts. The permission plan lists each grant as principal, securable, privilege and reason, at the lowest level that works: [[dbxfe-identity-leastpriv-concept|least privilege]]. The test matrix lists requests that must succeed and at least as many that must fail: the neighbouring table, the write, another supplier's rows, the unmasked column. [[dbxfe-identity-sod-concept|Separation of duties]] means different people request, approve, apply and audit the change. Notice that the wide plan in the second state passes every must-succeed test; only a must-fail row exposes it.
beats.hint: Which row in the matrix would stay green if the grant were too wide?

handbook.markdown:
**The plan.** One row per grant, never "access to the quality data":

| Principal | Securable | Privilege | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| supplier-portal (group holding sp-supplier-portal) | catalog quality | USE CATALOG | reach the schema |
| supplier-portal | schema quality.shared | USE SCHEMA | reach the table |
| supplier-portal | table quality.shared.supplier_rejections | SELECT | the only data the portal needs |

The table carries a row filter for the portal's own supplier and a mask on inspector emails. The service principal authenticates through workload identity federation or M2M, never a PAT, and has no secret scope READ it does not use.

**The matrix.** For every allowed request, add its neighbours as must-fail rows: a sibling table, a write on the same object, a read at the parent, another principal on the same object, rows outside the filter, and a masked column. Run every row as the real principal, never as an administrator, and record expected and observed side by side. A plan is accepted only when observed equals expected on every row; a wide plan usually passes all the allowed rows, so the denials are the evidence.

**Separation of duties.** The requester writes the need, the securable's owner approves, a platform administrator applies, and security reviews the permission-change audit row and the matrix output. Nobody approves their own request. Grants that give indirect power, such as membership of a group that holds MANAGE, trigger rights on a job running as a service principal, or tag assignment under an ABAC policy, go through the same path.

**Honest limits.** The governance review lab evaluates such a matrix with a small local evaluator; a locally evaluated table is not Unity Catalog enforcement, and the real principals must be tested in the workspace. No plan here certifies compliance.

beats.recap: A plan is narrow only when its must-fail tests fail; different people request, approve, apply and audit.

extensionCards.prompt: Who may make a job run as a service principal, and who may manage that principal?
extensionCards.answer: Principals holding the service principal's User role may set it as a job's run-as identity; the Manager role governs the principal itself.
extensionCards.explanation: Account access rules on a service principal distinguish two [[dbxfe-identity-extension-sp-roles-concept|service principal roles]]: roles/servicePrincipal.user allows using it, for example as a job's run-as identity, which the SDK documents as requiring that role, and roles/servicePrincipal.manager allows managing the principal and its rules. Both effectively hand over the principal's grants, so give User to the few who deploy its jobs, give Manager to its owners, and review both in the same access review as the data grants. The provider manages these rules authoritatively per object, overwriting rules it does not declare.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It exposes the indirect route to a service principal's privileges that a list of data grants never shows.

extensionCards.prompt: How long does a service principal's OAuth secret last, and how is it rotated without an outage?
extensionCards.answer: Without an explicit lifetime it lasts 730 days; create a second secret, switch the workload, confirm a token request, then delete the first.
extensionCards.explanation: The provider documents a default [[dbxfe-identity-extension-secret-lifetime-concept|OAuth secret lifetime]] of 730 days, settable in seconds at creation, and each secret reports create_time, expire_time and a status such as ACTIVE. Because several secrets can be listed for one principal, an overlap rotation avoids downtime: create the new secret, update the workload's secret store, watch a successful token request, then delete the old one. The provider's time_rotating pattern automates recreation, and a shorter lifetime limits how long a leaked secret stays useful.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It turns the commonest M2M outage, a lapsed secret, into a scheduled and observable change.

extensionCards.prompt: Can a workspace restrict who may create and use personal access tokens at all?
extensionCards.answer: Yes: using tokens is a permission, CAN_USE on the workspace's tokens object, and administrators can list and delete any user's tokens.
extensionCards.explanation: The provider's on-behalf-of token page grants [[dbxfe-identity-extension-token-permissions-concept|token usage permission]] as CAN_USE on the tokens authorization object and warns that declaring it overwrites the token permissions of existing groups such as users unless they are included. The SDK's token management API lets administrators get every token, all tokens of one user, and delete tokens for other users; each record shows its creator, expiry and an approximate last-used day. Restricting CAN_USE to an automation group and administrators removes the commonest leak source for everyone else.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It is a preventive control for token exposure rather than a clean-up after one.

extensionCards.prompt: Why might a query on system.access.audit fail or return nothing in a newly configured account?
extensionCards.answer: The access system schema must first be enabled by an account admin, and the reader needs privileges on it before any row is visible.
extensionCards.explanation: The provider documents system tables as a Databricks-hosted store of the account's operational data that an account admin must enable, schema by schema, with access as its example; [[dbxfe-identity-extension-system-schema-concept|system schema enablement]] is identified per metastore, some schemas are enabled automatically and some cannot be disabled. Until access is enabled the audit table cannot be queried, and because system schemas live in the system catalog, reading them follows Unity Catalog grants, so grant them to a security group. Rows can also lag the events they describe.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It stops an empty evidence query from being read as proof that nothing happened.

recap.title: Who authenticated, whose grants applied, what the logs prove
recap.markdown: **Every request answers three questions: who authenticated, whose permissions applied, and where it could fail.** People sign in with U2M; workloads are service principals using M2M or, better, workload identity federation; personal access tokens are bearer credentials to keep rare and short-lived. Groups carry grants, SCIM decides who exists, and a job's run-as identity, not whoever clicked Run, meets the grants. Filters and masks change answers without errors, and attribute-based policies follow tags. Audit rows tie identities to actions, and a leak is answered by revocation first. **Transfer challenge:** for a hospital's nightly export of lab results to an insurer, write the principal, its authentication method, the narrow grants, the secret scope, the row filter, a six-row test matrix and the audit query you would run after a leaked credential.

appliedTask.title: Review access for the supplier portal
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline will let supplier S-17 read its own rejected inspections through a portal hosted outside Databricks. Today a prototype uses a quality lead's personal access token with SELECT on the whole quality catalog, and inspector emails are visible. Write the threat and access review: the portal's identity and authentication method, the narrow permission plan, the row filter and column mask, secret handling, a test matrix with at least three must-fail rows, who requests, approves, applies and audits, and what you do about the prototype's token.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Identity: a service principal sp-supplier-portal in a supplier-portal group, authenticating with workload identity federation from the portal's platform, or OAuth M2M with its secret in that platform's secret store if federation is unavailable; no personal token. Plan: USE CATALOG on quality, USE SCHEMA on quality.shared and SELECT on the table quality.shared.supplier_rejections, all to the group. The table carries a row filter admitting the portal group only to supplier S-17 rows and a mask replacing inspector_email. Matrix: SELECT on supplier_rejections allowed; SELECT on quality.accepted.inspections denied; MODIFY on supplier_rejections denied; rows for S-22 zero; emails masked; Maya's SELECT on supplier_rejections denied. Duties: the supplier manager requests, the schema owner approves, a platform administrator applies, and security reviews the permission-change audit row and the matrix output. Prototype token: revoke it now, fix its exposure window, query the lead's audit rows inside it, and remove the catalog-wide grant.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer replaces a person's broad bearer token with a workload identity, narrows grants to one table, puts row and column protection in the data layer, and proves narrowness with must-fail tests run as the real principal; the old token is handled as an incident, not merely replaced.
